topic.title: FERC Suspends PJM's Backstop Power Auction: Does the AI Data-Center Grid Bottleneck Just Get Slower, or Does It Get Fixed?
topic.trigger: On September 29, 2026, FERC accepted but suspended for five months (to February 28, 2027) PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (Docket ER26-3380) -- the one-time capacity auction meant to close a 6,831 MW/5.6% reserve-margin shortfall -- citing unresolved cost-allocation, transmission-owner-exit and collateral issues, forcing PJM to cancel its planned September 30-October 21, 2026 backstop auction. This directly engages the watchlist event from this pipeline's August 28, 2026 report ('FERC ruling on PJM's ER26-3380 IRAS/BYONC filing'), though research found the BYONC curtailment-priority framework itself lives in a separate, still-undecided docket (ER26-3515).

questions.primary: Does FERC's September 29, 2026 order suspending PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (Docket ER26-3380) for five months -- while leaving PJM's companion BYONC/IRAS curtailment-priority filing (ER26-3515) still undecided past its requested effective date -- confirm, weaken, or simply prolong the firm-generation-capacity structural bottleneck this pipeline identified in PJM on August 28, 2026?
sub: What exactly did FERC accept, suspend, and refer to a paper hearing in its September 29, 2026 order, and why?
Is the BYONC-linked curtailment-priority mechanism central to the original thesis part of this order, or does it remain in the separate, still-pending ER26-3515 (IRAS) docket?
What does PJM's resulting cancellation of its September 30-October 21, 2026 backstop auction mean for closing the 6,831 MW/5.6% reserve-margin shortfall from the July 2026 Base Residual Auction?
How are PJM-exposed generators, consumer advocates and power suppliers reacting, and what does that reveal about who bears the cost and risk of new capacity for AI data centers?
Does this episode show regulatory/procedural uncertainty becoming as binding a constraint on new PJM capacity as physical generation scarcity itself?

thesis: FERC's September 29, 2026 order did not approve or reject the BYONC/IRAS curtailment-priority framework the August 28, 2026 report's watchlist event named -- that framework sits in a separate docket (ER26-3515) still undecided as of this report -- but it did suspend, for cost-allocation and collateral reasons, the directly related Reliability Backstop Procurement (ER26-3380) meant to close PJM's 6,831 MW capacity shortfall, forcing PJM to cancel its imminent backstop auction. The result is a partial, inconclusive outcome: PJM's underlying firm-generation-capacity shortfall (reaffirmed by a third consecutive Base Residual Auction shortfall) remains a genuine Structural Bottleneck, but the regulatory process meant to address it -- contested simultaneously by consumer advocates (too costly to ratepayers) and power suppliers (anti-competitive toward existing generation) -- has itself become a source of delay, adding a procedural layer to the bottleneck rather than resolving it.

facts.statement: On September 29, 2026, FERC issued an order accepting PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (Docket ER26-3380) in part but suspending it for five months to an effective date of February 28, 2027, subject to refund and the outcome of further proceedings.

FERC found that aspects of PJM's proposal -- cost allocation for the backstop procurement, the treatment of costs if a transmission owner exits PJM before those costs are recouped, and collateral requirements imposed on load-serving entities -- may be unjust and unreasonable, and set a paper hearing on those issues while 'strongly encouraging' PJM to propose fixes quickly.

FERC separately found PJM's proposed collateral requirements for power suppliers (as opposed to load-serving entities) appropriate, and suggested that if a transmission owner exits PJM before backstop costs are recouped, those costs should fall to load-serving entities within that transmission zone rather than to the transmission owner.
FERC Chair Laura Swett, in a concurring statement, said PJM's proposal was filed at the last minute, leaving the Commission no time "to rehabilitate the mess we received."

Following the order, PJM suspended its planned Reliability Backstop Procurement auction, which had been scheduled to accept supply offers from September 30 through October 21, 2026, to address the capacity shortfall identified in PJM's 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction.

PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (ER26-3380) was originally filed with FERC on July 31, 2026, proposing a one-time capacity procurement to close the 6,831 MW shortfall left when PJM's July 14, 2026 Base Residual Auction for the 2028/2029 delivery year cleared below PJM's reliability target.

PJM's July 14, 2026 Base Residual Auction for the 2028/2029 delivery year procured 138,318 MW of unforced capacity (UCAP) and cleared at the $325/MW-day price cap -- a reserve margin of 14.7%, or 6,831 MW (5.6%) below PJM's reliability requirement, the third consecutive delivery year the auction has cleared short of target.

A separate but related PJM filing -- the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) and Large Load Registry, filed August 13, 2026 under Docket ER26-3515 -- contains the Bring-Your-Own-New-Capacity (BYONC) mechanism and curtailment-priority framework central to this pipeline's August 28, 2026 report; PJM requested an effective date of October 12, 2026, but no FERC order on ER26-3515 had been issued as of this report.

PJM's own Independent Market Monitor (Monitoring Analytics, led by Joseph Bowring) filed a protest on September 3, 2026 arguing the IRAS filing (ER26-3515) "has not been supported as just and reasonable" and calling it "a convoluted, inconsistent, confusing proposal" that should be rejected.

The Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA) also protested the IRAS filing on September 3, 2026, arguing the BYONC requirement would unduly discriminate against existing generation resources, distort capacity-market price signals, increase long-run consumer costs, and undermine investor confidence in PJM's market design, while stating it did not oppose the Large Load Registry itself.

Maryland's Office of People's Counsel protested the Reliability Backstop Procurement (ER26-3380), estimating that if the anticipated data centers behind the capacity shortfall are delayed, canceled, or relocated, the RBP's costs could still fall on residential ratepayers -- roughly $483 million over 15 years for Potomac Edison customers and $79 million for Baltimore Gas and Electric customers -- and quoting People's Counsel David S. Lapp that the filing "is rife with admissions that there may be no capacity shortfall that causes reliability issues."

Shares of Constellation Energy fell approximately 4.9% on the day of FERC's order, with NRG Energy and Talen Energy also declining; TD Cowen analysts described the regulatory outcome as creating "acute" uncertainty for PJM-exposed generators.

inferences.statement: Because FERC's September 29, 2026 order addressed only the Reliability Backstop Procurement (ER26-3380) -- a capacity-auction cost-allocation mechanism -- and not the companion IRAS/BYONC curtailment-priority filing (ER26-3515) that this pipeline's August 28, 2026 report centered on, the watchlist event has only partially resolved: the capacity-procurement path to closing PJM's shortfall has been delayed, while the curtailment-priority policy that determines which large loads get cut first remains undecided and contested by both PJM's own market monitor and the power-suppliers' trade association.

Because opposition to PJM's filings comes simultaneously from a consumer advocate (warning the backstop procurement overcharges ratepayers for capacity that may not be needed) and from merchant generators/power suppliers (warning the curtailment-priority mechanism unfairly favors new, BYONC-backed capacity over existing resources), PJM's proposed rules are being squeezed from opposite directions, making a materially watered-down final framework at least as likely as approval substantially as filed.

Because the underlying reserve-margin shortfall (5.6%, the third consecutive shortfall year) persists even as the clearing price edged down slightly from the prior year's cap, the physical generation-capacity scarcity behind this story appears to be stabilizing at a severe-but-not-accelerating level, while the newly added five-month regulatory suspension is, for now, a larger incremental delay to new capacity reaching the market than the underlying auction dynamics themselves.

unknowns: Whether FERC's eventual post-hearing ruling on the Reliability Backstop Procurement (ER26-3380) will approve PJM's cost-allocation and collateral provisions largely as filed, require material changes, or reject them is unknown.

FERC had not issued an order on the companion IRAS/Large Load Registry/BYONC filing (ER26-3515) as of this report, despite PJM's requested October 12, 2026 effective date; the timing and substance of that order are unknown.
Whether PJM will file a revised Reliability Backstop Procurement proposal quickly, as FERC 'strongly encouraged,' or allow the five-month suspension to run its full course, is unknown.

The precise distribution of Reliability Backstop Procurement costs across all PJM zones and states beyond the Maryland-specific estimates cited by the Office of People's Counsel has not been disclosed.

All primary FERC, PJM, and company-investor-relations domains attempted (ferc.gov, elibrary.ferc.gov, pjm.com, insidelines.pjm.com, utilitydive.com, rtoinsider.com, bloomberg.com, monitoringanalytics.com, epsa.org, opc.maryland.gov) were blocked by the research environment's egress proxy; facts rely on convergent search-result snippets and their characterization of underlying filings rather than direct verification of the full original documents.

bottlenecks.node: Firm dispatchable generation capacity in PJM
bottlenecks.expansion_time: 3+ years (gas turbines), longer where financing/siting lags
bottlenecks.rationale: PJM's Base Residual Auction has now cleared short of its reliability target for a third consecutive delivery year (5.6%/6,831 MW short in 2028/2029), reaffirming the August 28, 2026 finding; the backstop mechanism meant to close this gap has itself just been delayed five months, showing new firm capacity cannot be added quickly through either the ordinary market or emergency procurement.

bottlenecks.node: FERC/PJM cost-allocation and curtailment-priority rulemaking process (ER26-3380 and ER26-3515)
bottlenecks.rationale: Market participants' demand for regulatory certainty is high, and that certainty can only come from this specific, slow adjudicatory process (no substitute path), but as an administrative rationing mechanism rather than a market with pricing power or profit capture, it is honestly classified Neutral rather than a bottleneck in the strict commercial sense -- consistent with the August 28, 2026 report's treatment of PJM's policy framework as a rationing mechanism that reveals, rather than is, the underlying bottleneck.

bottlenecks.node: BYONC-contracted dedicated generation for large loads
bottlenecks.rationale: Well-capitalized developers can contract dedicated generation to avoid curtailment exposure (as this pipeline's September 6, 2026 report documented with Vistra-Amazon), and EPSA's protest confirms this path is contested precisely because it is viable, not because it is physically constrained -- consistent with a Growth Area rather than a Structural Bottleneck.

bear_case.argument: FERC explicitly 'strongly encouraged' PJM to refile a fix quickly and said doing so could avoid the hearing altogether, suggesting this is a procedural correction rather than a structural rejection, and the backstop mechanism could still take effect close to its original intent well before the February 28, 2027 deadline.

The 2028/2029 auction's reserve-margin shortfall (5.6%) and clearing price ($325/MW-day) both came in slightly better than the prior year's cap ($333.44/MW-day), suggesting the underlying physical scarcity, while real, is not visibly worsening each cycle.

EPSA's protest of the BYONC/IRAS filing argues existing generation resources are being unfairly disadvantaged relative to new BYONC-backed capacity -- the opposite problem from a pure capacity shortage -- indicating the dispute is partly about market-design fairness, not solely about physical supply constraints.
If hyperscaler AI capital-expenditure growth decelerates, pressure on PJM's reserve margin and on these contested dockets could ease independent of how FERC ultimately rules.

Large, well-capitalized developers already have a working alternative -- BYONC-style dedicated generation contracts, as Vistra's Comanche Peak-Amazon deal demonstrated -- so even an unfavorable or delayed outcome on these PJM dockets may not bind the best-capitalized AI infrastructure developers as tightly as it binds smaller players or ratepayers.

kill_conditions.condition: FERC resolves the Reliability Backstop Procurement paper hearing quickly and approves a revised proposal well before the February 28, 2027 suspension deadline, allowing PJM's backstop auction to proceed close to its original schedule
kill_conditions.metric: Timing and substance of FERC's post-hearing order on ER26-3380
kill_conditions.threshold: Order issued and a backstop auction conducted within 90 days of any PJM refiling

kill_conditions.condition: FERC approves PJM's companion IRAS/BYONC filing (ER26-3515) substantially as filed despite the Market Monitor's and EPSA's protests, confirming the curtailment-priority framework is not itself contested enough to be weakened
kill_conditions.threshold: Approved without material change to the BYONC curtailment-priority mechanism

kill_conditions.condition: PJM's reserve-margin shortfall closes in a subsequent Base Residual Auction
kill_conditions.metric: PJM BRA cleared capacity vs. reliability requirement
kill_conditions.threshold: A subsequent auction clears at or above the 20% reliability target with no shortfall
